subject: chemistry
title: Mixtures and separation techniques
key_idea: A **mixture** is two or more substances that are not chemically combined, so each keeps its own properties. Mixtures are separated by physical processes: filtration, crystallisation, simple distillation, fractional distillation and chromatography. No new substances are made.

blocks.text: A mixture can contain elements, compounds or both. This section covers how a mixture differs from a compound.

items.meaning: Two or more elements or compounds not chemically combined together.
A method that separates substances without a chemical reaction. No new substances are made.

items: The chemical properties of each substance in a mixture are unchanged.
The substances are not in a fixed ratio.
Examples: air, sea water, ink, crude oil.
A mixture is separated by physical processes. A compound can only be separated by a chemical reaction.
In a mixture the substances are not chemically combined.
Each substance keeps its own chemical properties.
Separating a mixture does not make new substances.

blocks.text: Each technique uses a different property of the substances. Pick the method from the property that differs.

rows: An insoluble solid from a liquid
The solid is too big to pass through the filter paper. The liquid passes through.
A soluble solid from its solution
Water is evaporated, and the solid forms crystals as the solution cools.
A liquid from a solution with dissolved solid
The liquid evaporates and is condensed again. The solid stays behind.
A mixture of liquids that mix together
The liquids have different boiling points.
Coloured substances, such as the dyes in ink
The substances move different distances up the paper.

items: Filtration removes an insoluble solid, such as sand or unreacted metal. Dissolved ions pass through the filter.
To crystallise: heat the solution until crystals start to form (crystallisation point). Do not heat it to dryness.
Then leave the solution to cool and crystallise. Filter off the crystals and dry them.

items.text: The solution is heated and the water evaporates.
The vapour cools in the condenser and turns to a liquid.
Pure water collects in the beaker. The salt is left in the flask.

items: Cold water flows through the outside of the condenser. It warms up as it removes heat from the vapour.
The thermometer shows 100 °C while pure water distils.
The mixture is heated and passes up a fractionating column.
The liquid with the lowest boiling point reaches the top first and is condensed and collected.
Example: ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) is collected before water (100 °C).
Crude oil is separated into fractions in the same way.
Draw a pencil line near the bottom of the paper and put a spot of ink on it. Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent.
Stand the paper in a solvent such as water, with the line above the solvent level.
The solvent soaks up the paper and carries the dyes with it. Different dyes travel different distances.
Each separate spot is a different substance. A pure substance gives one spot.

diagram.alt: Sort each separation into filtration, crystallisation or distillation.

items.text: Sand from a mixture of sand and water
Copper sulfate crystals from copper sulfate solution
Ethanol from a mixture of ethanol and water
Unreacted magnesium from magnesium chloride solution
Solid sodium chloride from sodium chloride solution

items: Filtration removes insoluble solids. Crystallisation recovers dissolved solids.
Distillation separates liquids using their boiling points. The lowest boiling point comes off first.
Distillation: the liquid evaporates, then the vapour condenses.
Chromatography separates coloured substances by how far each moves up the paper.

blocks.text: To plan a separation, look at which substances are soluble in water, which are liquids and what their boiling points are.

items.text: Add water to the mixture and stir. The salt dissolves. The sand does not.
The sand stays on the filter paper. The salt solution passes through. Wash and dry the sand.
Heat the salt solution to concentrate it, then leave it to cool so crystals form.
Filter off the crystals and dry them.

items: Insoluble solid and soluble solid: add water, filter, then evaporate or crystallise the filtrate.
Solid dissolved in a liquid, and you want the liquid: simple distillation.
Two liquids that mix, with different boiling points: fractional distillation.
Iron and sulfur: use a magnet, because only iron is magnetic.
Do the steps in a sensible order: filter before you distil or crystallise.
Name the property that makes each method work, such as solubility or boiling point.

checks.q: State the difference between a mixture and a compound.
checks.a: In a mixture the substances are not chemically combined and keep their own properties. In a compound the elements are chemically combined in fixed proportions.

checks.q: Name the method used to separate ethanol (boiling point 78 °C) from water (boiling point 100 °C). Which one is collected first?
checks.a: Fractional distillation. Ethanol is collected first because it has the lower boiling point.

checks.q: Describe how to obtain crystals of copper sulfate from copper sulfate solution.
checks.a: Heat the solution to evaporate some of the water. Leave it to cool so that crystals form.

worked_example.question:
A student distils a sample of salt solution to produce pure water using standard distillation apparatus.

Describe how the process of distillation produces pure water from salt solution.
answer_points: The water evaporates (boils or vaporises is also accepted).
The vapour cools in the condenser.
The vapour condenses, turning to a liquid.
The pure water collects in the beaker.
worked_example.tip: Any four of these score one mark each. Use the order evaporate, then condense.

worked_example.question:
A sample of rock salt contains a mixture of sodium chloride and some insoluble substances.
The rock salt is added to water and the mixture stirred.
The mixture is then filtered to obtain a filtrate of sodium chloride solution.

Describe how a sample of pure, dry sodium chloride crystals can be obtained from the filtrate.
answer_points: Heat the solution to concentrate it.
Leave the solution to cool, or in a warm place, so that it crystallises.
Filter off the crystals, or decant the liquid from them.
Pat the crystals dry between filter papers, or dry them in an oven.
worked_example.tip: Any three score one mark each. If no other marks are scored, the word crystallisation alone gets one mark.

worked_example.question:
A student has a mixture of three substances.

Sand: insoluble in water, melting point 1710 °C, boiling point 2230 °C.
Sodium chloride: soluble in water, melting point 801 °C, boiling point 1413 °C.
Water: melting point 0 °C, boiling point 100 °C.

Describe how the student can separate the mixture to get pure samples of all three substances.

Explain why each method of separation works.
answer_points: This works because sand is insoluble in water and sodium chloride is soluble.
The solid sodium chloride stays in the flask and the pure water condenses.
worked_example.tip: Keep to the order: filter, then distil. The wrong order scores at most 3 marks, and each method needs its reason.
